passage: Fatima could tell the whole story of the Viking raid on Lindisfarne as if she had been in the boat: the cold spray, the bells, the monks running. In class discussions in her Oslo school, everyone listened. But in timed tests her answers came out short and misspelled, and she always ran out of time halfway. Her history mark said average. Her head said she knew everything. Lars, the learning support teacher, noticed the gap. "Would you do an assessment with the school psychologist? It would show how you learn best." The report came back weeks later. Fatima got extra time and could type her answers. In the next test she wrote four full pages. When the mark came back, she read the comment twice: "This is what you really know."

qa.q: What could Fatima type after the assessment?
qa.a: Her answers, and she also got extra time.

qa.q: What does it suggest that Fatima's head 'said she knew everything'?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated, because she knew the history well but the timed, written tests didn't show it.

qa.q: What was the key step that changed Fatima's results?
qa.a: Lars suggested an assessment, which led to extra time and typing, so her knowledge could show.

qa.q: How might Lars see Fatima's four pages compared with her old tests?
qa.a: Lars would see that her real ability was there all along and only the test conditions hid it.

grounding: It shows a teenager who tells stories brilliantly but struggles with spelling and reading speed under time limits, and how an assessment and accommodations show what she truly knows.

passage: The exam room for students with extra time was a small classroom on the second floor, with a fan that clicked. "You okay?" Pranav asked at the door. He'd come up just to walk Eshaan in. "Honestly? My hands are shaking. Last year I only finished half the paper." "Last year you didn't have the extra time or the reader." The reader was a young woman from the school office who would read the questions aloud. Eshaan sat down. When she read question four, about a village during a flood, he closed his eyes and saw it: the brown water, the roofs, a goat on a door. He wrote it out in rough spelling, but full. Afterwards Pranav waited on the steps. "Well?" "I finished," Eshaan said. "For the first time, I finished."

qa.q: What did the reader from the school office do?
qa.a: She read the questions aloud to Eshaan.

qa.q: Why were Eshaan's hands shaking before the exam?
qa.a: He was anxious because last year he only finished half the paper.

qa.q: What difference did the permitted support make?
qa.a: With extra time and a reader, Eshaan could picture and write full answers and finished the paper for the first time.

qa.q: How does Pranav show he sees Eshaan's struggle?
qa.a: Pranav walks him in, reminds him that the conditions are different now, and waits afterwards to hear how it went.

grounding: It shows a teenager who thinks in pictures but struggles with reading speed, whose permitted accommodations let him show what he knows.

passage:
Note from Manjula, English teacher, Class 10.
Lalit tells the best stories in the class. When we read the chapter on the flood, he retold it with such detail that two students gasped. His notebooks are full of diagrams and little drawings of every scene. But in timed tests he writes half a page, the spellings scrambled, and hands in the paper with his head down. Last week he said, "I know it, ma'am. I just can't get it out fast enough."
I spoke to his parents that afternoon and suggested an assessment. The report came yesterday. With the board's permission, he will now get extra time and a reader in exams. In Friday's practice test with extra time, he scored his highest mark this year.

qa.q: What did Lalit's notebooks contain?
qa.a: They are full of diagrams and little drawings of every scene.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel when handing in timed tests?
qa.a: He feels discouraged and ashamed, handing in the paper with his head down because he cannot write what he knows fast enough.

qa.q: Why was suggesting an assessment the right step?
qa.a: It showed the real difficulty and led to permitted extra time and a reader, so his marks could reflect what he actually knows.

qa.q: How might Lalit's parents feel about the practice test result?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and proud, seeing clear proof that Lalit knows the work when given fair conditions.

grounding: Shows a teenager who thinks in pictures and tells stories brilliantly but struggles with spelling and speed under time limits, helped by assessment and accommodations.

passage:
Monday.
Prelims history paper today. I KNEW the answers. I could see the whole battle like a film in my head: the river, the horses, who moved first. But three hours wasn't enough. I wrote slow, crossed out spellings, and the bell rang with two questions blank. Baljeet asked how it went and I said "fine" and walked off.
Then this evening Mummy and I went to the clinic for the assessment the school counsellor suggested. The psychologist had me read, spell, do puzzles. At the end she said I reason really well, and that I can apply for extra time in the boards.
I don't feel stupid tonight. For the first time I feel like the marks might finally match my head.
Vaibhav

qa.q: How many questions did Vaibhav leave blank?
qa.a: Vaibhav left two questions blank when the bell rang.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when Baljeet asked about the paper?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt frustrated and embarrassed, saying "fine" and walking off because the answers were known but not written in time.

qa.q: What step made the difference for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Going for the assessment the counsellor suggested, which showed strong reasoning and opened the way to apply for extra time in the boards.

qa.q: What might Baljeet think when Vaibhav walks off after saying "fine"?
qa.a: Baljeet might feel confused or brushed off, not knowing how upset Vaibhav really was about the paper.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees history like a film but struggles with spelling and speed under time limits, and gets an assessment leading to permitted extra time.

passage:
Parveen could stand on the grain-market steps in Raichur and tell a ghost story that made the whole lane go quiet. She saw every scene like a film in her head.
But in the half-yearly exam she finished only two of five answers. Her spellings wandered; she read each question three times. The paper came back red. "You know this," her friend Charu said. "You explained photosynthesis to me with drawings."
Parveen wanted to tear the paper. "Maybe I'm just slow."
Charu's mother, a nurse, told them the district hospital could assess her reading and writing. It took two visits and a long form. After that, the school approved extra time and a reader for the board exams.
In the prelims, Parveen finished every answer. Her marks jumped. "That's what I actually know," she said, staring.

qa.q: How many answers did Parveen finish in the half-yearly exam?
qa.a: Only two of five answers.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when the paper came back red?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and discouraged, wanting to tear the paper and wondering if she was just slow.

qa.q: What turned things around for Parveen?
qa.a: An assessment at the district hospital led to permitted extra time and a reader, so her exam marks could show what she really knew.

qa.q: How does Charu see Parveen's ability?
qa.a: Charu believes in her, having seen her explain photosynthesis with drawings, and is sure the red marks do not show what Parveen knows.

grounding: Parveen thinks in pictures and tells stories brilliantly but struggles under time limits until an assessment and permitted accommodations show what she knows.
